basis: These links are Lensatic’s own reading of each play. No publisher prints a crosswalk from the plays to these frameworks, so nothing here is counted as an overlap.

story.title: Agents are the new insiders
story.line: An AI agent with broad access acts like a privileged insider, at machine speed. Give it an identity, an owner and least privilege, then put a boundary around it that it cannot talk its way past.
story.short: An AI agent with broad access is a privileged insider. Start here.

links.line: The play turns periodic assessment into a loop: penetration testing, red team exercises and continuous monitoring.
Improvements come from tests and exercises, and what runs is watched all the time.
Humans in command is a stated oversight role for people working with AI systems.
Red and purple work is planned and scored against ATT&CK’s techniques.
The same loop covers attacks on your own AI, which ATLAS catalogs.
People own the decisions: defined oversight roles, leadership that answers for the risk, documented human oversight and the means to switch a system off.
Accountability stays with named leaders and roles.
An agent that proposes is not the one that approves, and autonomy widens only as privilege is granted.
The fundamentals the play builds first: know your systems and data, generate the logs, and analyze and correlate events before automating the work.
Triage discipline, tuned monitoring and incident handling are the ground AI multiplies.
The play’s three ways AI is turned on its owner: input threats, compromised suppliers and poisoned data.
AI brings new suppliers, and the risks of third-party data and models are mapped and governed.
An emulation chain as the play describes it: scan, exploit a public-facing application or phish, with AI as an obtained capability, then execute.

Your own AI attack surface, tested: prompt injection, jailbreaks, RAG poisoning, model evasion, the AI supply chain, poisoned agent tools and rug pulls, and autonomous reconnaissance and orchestration.
Penetration testing by an independent team, red team exercises, vulnerability scanning and developer testing.
Security and resilience are evaluated, by people who did not build the system, with the test sets and tools documented.
Vulnerabilities are validated and not only found, and exercises feed improvement.
Triage is the Detect and Respond outcomes at volume: monitor, analyze, correlate, bring in threat intelligence, then triage and prioritize.
Monitoring with automated real-time analysis, audit review, automated incident handling, threat hunting and flaw remediation.
The department’s SIEM, analytics, orchestrated response and security operations capabilities are the ones triage agents work in.
The analysis a detection agent runs, by D3FEND’s names: network traffic, process, user behavior and message analysis.
The alert, the log line and the suspect file are attacker-shaped input: prompt injection, and exploiting an automated pipeline that processes artifacts.
A defensive agent’s quality drifts, so it is monitored in production and its risks tracked over time.
Red team exercises joined to continuous monitoring, control assessment and tests of the monitoring tools themselves.
Improvements identified from evaluations and exercises, with each missed detection analyzed.
The deepfake help desk example ends in the account: phishing by voice, then valid accounts, account manipulation and a changed authentication process.
ATT&CK coverage alone misses the AI techniques the loop must also run: deepfakes, impersonation and prompt injection.
Each gap the loop finds closes with a countermeasure, which D3FEND names.
Security is evaluated again and again, and what is learned goes back into the system.
A maturity ladder beside a maturity model: the CISA model’s cross-cutting capabilities climb the same way, from manual to automated to dynamic.
The Automation and Orchestration pillar names machine learning, artificial intelligence and orchestrated response as capabilities.
How much oversight a level needs follows the risk the organization will accept.
Assess and baseline first, improve from the evaluation, review performance at each gate, and set the risk appetite before autonomy grows.
A baseline assessment, a plan of action with milestones, continuous monitoring and a risk management strategy.
A phased path with an exit gate at every phase follows the RMF’s own shape: prepare, then step by step to monitoring.
Coverage against ATT&CK is the roadmap’s baseline measure.
Who owns what, the resources, the workforce and the training are the Govern and Awareness outcomes.
A named program leader, resources, a security workforce, role-based training and an acquisition process for build or buy.
Roles and lines of communication for AI risk, training for the people who carry them, and policy for third-party AI.
Performance is evaluated and reviewed, improvements come from operations, and the scope of events is understood.
Measures of performance, continuous monitoring and incident monitoring give the numbers the play pairs for speed and quality.
Metrics are chosen, their fitness is reviewed, performance is measured in conditions like deployment, and gains or declines are tracked.
Coverage is counted as the share of in-scope ATT&CK techniques with a tested detection.
One sequenced list of every action is a plan of action and milestones with a risk response for each item.
Risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned and tracked.
Treatment of AI risk is prioritized, and the responses are planned and documented.
A layered architecture with security engineering principles, boundaries, controlled flows between layers and validated input.
The system’s tasks and components are defined, each component’s controls are identified, and behavior and security are measured at the evaluation layer.
Data flows are mapped, environments are protected, and data in use is protected.
The attacker’s view, layer by layer: the prompt, the retrieval store, the supply chain, the tools and the model itself.
Every layer applies the zero trust principle: no request is trusted for where it comes from.
Hosting as an external service, contingency and backup, protection from denial of service, resource availability, data at rest and log capacity.
Resilience, capacity, data at rest, backups and an inventory of supplier services.
Token economics have an adversary’s side: cost harvesting and denial of AI service.
Hosting an agent on a cloud service for a federal customer brings FedRAMP in.

The plumbing by control: boundary protection that denies by default, proxied and filtered egress, flow enforcement, traffic monitored for covert exfiltration, service identity, least privilege, key management, protected transit and isolation.
Data flow mapping, macro and micro segmentation, all traffic logged and least privileged access.
The Networks pillar’s functions and access management, applied to an agent enclave.
Outbound and inbound filtering, network isolation, DNS allowlisting, traffic analysis and execution isolation.
Networks protected from unauthorized use, data in transit protected, networks monitored and permissions enforced.
Egress control and segmentation are how the zero trust definition becomes physical.
The line between IT and OT is a boundary with isolated components and enforced flows; safe mode, fail-safe procedures and a known failure state put safety first.
Protected environments, resilience in adverse conditions, the physical environment monitored and assets ranked by mission impact.
Safety is evaluated, human oversight is defined, and the system can be disengaged.
Zero trust in OT starts at segmentation.
A control system is authorized under the RMF like any other federal system.
The play anchors itself to the AI RMF: requirements understood, the process transparent and reviewed, roles clear, risks documented and monitoring planned.
Authorize, scope, log and review: accounts, least privilege, event logging and review, continuous monitoring and change control for every suppression and tuning change.
Policy is set and enforced, outcomes are reviewed, authorities are clear and permissions are managed.
Mapping each control to a recognized framework is what makes the evidence usable in an authorization.
Legal, regulatory and contractual requirements are understood and managed, and the strategy is adjusted to cover them.
Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and documented, and incidents are identified and communicated.
The audit trail the obligations ask for: a risk strategy, retained records, incident reporting and a documented plan.
The play likens the management system standard for AI to ISO/IEC 27001, the one for information security.
Authorization to operate, and continuous authorization, are the RMF’s Authorize and Monitor steps.
A cloud service an agent runs on needs FedRAMP certification for federal use.
The department’s Impact Levels set where data of each sensitivity may be processed.
The control spine: authorization, continuous monitoring, the system security plan, accounts and service identities for agents, and the boundary an authorization draws.
Agents as non-human identities belong in the integrated ICAM platform, under privileged access management and least privilege, with continuous monitoring and ongoing authorizations.
Controlled unclassified information on a contractor’s systems brings SP 800-171 in.
CMMC is how the department checks a contractor’s handling of that information.
Suppliers are known and ranked, requirements go into contracts, due diligence comes before the relationship, and authenticity is assessed before use.
The acquisition process, external services, supply chain controls, provenance, supplier reviews, component authenticity and a component inventory, which an AI bill of materials extends.
Third-party AI risk is governed, contingencies are planned, components are mapped, and pre-trained models are monitored.
What diligence is looking for: a compromised supply chain, poisoned training data, a rug pull and inflated reputation.
For a cloud vendor, FedRAMP certification is evidence a federal buyer can reuse.
A model of how the system is attacked draws on ATLAS: prompt injection and jailbreaks, tool invocation, context poisoning, the supply chain and a user who runs what the repository tells them to.
Start from the use case: intended purpose and setting, the task, the likelihood and size of each impact, then security evaluated.
Risk assessment, developer testing with threat modeling, engineering principles and the security architecture.
Threats are identified, their likelihood and impact recorded, and both used to set priorities.
The classic techniques still apply to an AI system’s ordinary parts.
The taxonomy the play opens with: prompt injection, data and memory poisoning, deepfakes and identity theft, and the lethal trifecta’s way out through an inference API or an agent’s tools.
AI as a capability adversaries obtain, and the phishing and valid accounts it sharpens.
Threat intelligence is received, threats are recorded, and both are used in analysis.
A threat awareness program, risk assessment and the advisories that feed them.
Emergent AI risks are tracked, and incidents are identified and shared.
Intelligence is received, turned into recorded threats, used in analysis, and what hunting finds becomes a detection.
A threat awareness program with automated sharing, threat hunting, indicators of compromise, advisories and contact with security groups.
Threat intelligence integration is a capability of the Visibility and Analytics pillar.
What CTI tells red to emulate and blue to hunt begins before the intrusion: scanning, gathering identities and obtaining capabilities.
Jailbreaks tracked as a class of intelligence, and reconnaissance that runs on its own.
Every agent gets its own account, an owner and least privilege, credentials that are never embedded, actions that can be attributed to it, and the monitoring a privileged user gets.

The outcomes the play asks for: identities for services are managed and authenticated, permissions are least privilege and reviewed, activity is monitored, and each identity is managed through its life cycle.
The play treats an agent as a user: privileged access management, behavioral identity, least privileged access, continuous authentication and entity behavior analytics.
The Identity pillar’s functions, read for an identity that is not a person.
Inventory every AI system, retire it safely, name who answers for it, monitor it in production and examine its accountability.
What a subverted agent does with an insider’s access: poisoned context and memory, a changed configuration, harvested credentials, and tools invoked to move data out.
The classic insider techniques an agent’s identity is open to: valid accounts, account manipulation and stolen or replayed application tokens.
Countermeasures by name: authenticate the agent, rotate and revoke its credentials, scope its permissions and analyze its behavior.
The play’s zero trust for agents starts from this definition: verify every request, whoever or whatever makes it.

Deterministic boundaries first: deny outbound traffic by default, prevent exfiltration, isolate the process, limit function, monitor, patch by risk, and stop the system automatically when a threshold trips.
The environment is protected from unauthorized use, unauthorized software cannot run, the runtime is monitored, vulnerabilities are validated, and incidents are contained.
Macro and micro segmentation put the boundary in the network; automated patching and orchestrated response act at the agent’s speed.
Segmentation and threat protection, where the model asks how far an agent’s workload is isolated.
The means to disengage or deactivate a system, a response to an unknown risk, security and resilience evaluated, and human oversight that is defined and not assumed.
What the boundary has to hold against: prompt injection, exfiltration and destruction through an agent’s tools, escape to the host and sandbox evasion.
The play’s own worked example in ATT&CK’s words is unsecured credentials sent to a web service. A shell and an escape to the host are what the sandbox is there to stop.
Execution isolation, network isolation, outbound traffic filtering, system call filtering and allowlists, then process termination when a breaker trips.
The play follows Respond and Recover: execute the plan, triage, find the root cause, preserve the records, contain, eradicate, restore and verify, with the plan kept current.
Incident handling, automated and able to disable the system, with a plan that is tested, logs that are protected and kept, recovery, and accounts disabled fast.
Respond to an unknown risk, deactivate the system, track and communicate incidents, and plan for a third party’s failure.
Fast containment by D3FEND’s names: terminate the process, revoke the credential, lock the account, end the session and isolate the network.
The agent as the incident: injected, its context poisoned, its tools used to destroy data, its configuration changed.
Security operations and incident response, with orchestration to act at the agent’s speed.

The supply chain family, read as counterintelligence: a plan, controls, provenance, operations security, tamper detection, component authenticity, integrity checks, signed components and control of the configuration files that steer an agent.
A supply chain risk program inside enterprise risk, supplier risk understood, suppliers in incident planning and authenticity checked before use.
How an adversary uses the AI supply chain: compromise it, poison the data, publish poisoned artifacts, change or read an agent’s configuration, pull the rug, poison a tool or manipulate the model.
Supply chain compromise through dependencies or the product itself, poisoned pipelines and trusted relationships.
Third-party components are mapped, monitored and governed, pre-trained models included.
Secure software development and software risk management are capabilities of the Applications and Workloads pillar.
Work with people outside the team: feedback from outside is sought, testing and incident sharing are enabled, and measurement is informed by domain experts.
Threat intelligence comes from sharing forums, and outside stakeholders are understood.
Contact with security groups and a threat awareness program are how a program hears from the frontier.
The play’s first reference, by its four functions.
CSF 2.0 is the common language the play uses for outcomes.
The CIS Controls are the play’s prioritized safeguards.
ATLAS is the play’s catalog of attacks on AI.
Zero trust for agents rests on the SP 800-207 definition.
NIST’s Cyber AI Profile joins CSF 2.0 to AI.
Independent research is the play’s counterweight to vendor claims: assessors who did not build the system, documented test methods and outside experts.
The papers the play cites test attacks that ATLAS catalogs.
Research is a source of threat intelligence.

The documented intrusions in ATT&CK’s words: scanning, exploiting public-facing applications, valid accounts, remote services, data from repositories and exfiltration to web services, with AI as the obtained capability.
And in ATLAS’s: autonomous orchestration, reconnaissance and attack-path adaptation, by way of a jailbreak and generated commands.
What each case proves is used: lessons from tests, root cause from incidents and threats recorded.
The cases cover red team exercises, incident handling and threat hunting.
The play’s risks as ATLAS techniques: prompt injection and exfiltration through tools, memory poisoning, tool invocation, self-replicating prompts and agents talking to agents.
Impacts are sized, treatment is prioritized, residual risk is written down, a safety-first habit is kept, privacy risk is examined and legal requirements are understood.
The play names AU-10 and AU-9 for attribution; least privilege, risk assessment, awareness and an insider threat program answer the rest.
Risk appetite is stated, risks are scored one way, impact and likelihood are recorded, and people are trained against overreliance.
A tool stack starts as an inventory of software and services, then monitoring and correlation.
A component inventory, an acquisition process, integrated monitoring tools and penetration testing tools.
Orchestrated response, standard APIs and a SIEM are the capabilities the stack fills.
The AI security tools in the play test for techniques ATLAS names.
One of the play’s tools maps its work to the Cyber AI Profile, among other frameworks.
The attack terms the glossary defines, by identifier: prompt injection, jailbreak, RAG poisoning, training data poisoning and model evasion.
TTP, tactic and technique are ATT&CK’s words.
The glossary’s federal terms point at this control catalog.
The glossary’s terms for controlled unclassified information point at SP 800-171.
The glossary’s cloud authorization terms are FedRAMP’s.
ATO and continuous ATO are RMF terms.
Zero trust is defined in SP 800-207.
A self-study path is the training outcome, for everyone and for specialized roles.
Literacy training with practical exercises, role-based training, and red team exercises to practice on.
AI risk training for staff and partners, and proficiency of the people who operate the system.
The path names ATT&CK among the frameworks to know cold.
The path names ATLAS among the frameworks to know cold, for attacks on AI.
The index names CSF 2.0 among its framework sources.
The index names the AI RMF among its framework sources.
The index lists the federal control catalog among its federal standards.
The index’s zero trust sources start from this definition.
The index’s zero trust sources follow the lineage on to the CISA model.
The index’s zero trust sources end at the department’s strategy.
FedRAMP is among its federal sources.
ATT&CK is among its threat sources.
ATLAS is among the index’s threat sources.
